opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think anyone is ever fully "ready" to start a company, especially in a field like embodied intelligence where so much is still unsettled. But in early 2023 a few things came together that made me feel the timing was right, even if I wasn't certain.

The first was technical. For years my research had focused on robot perception, 3D vision, and manipulation, with a lot of work on simulation and synthetic data. For a long time there was a real gap between what we could do in the lab and what could work reliably in the real world. Around late 2022 and early 2023 I felt that gap starting to close. Large models were showing real generalization, and on our side, simulation-based data generation and sim-to-real transfer had matured enough that I could see a path to robots that generalize, not just robots that perform well in carefully staged demos. Once you can see a path like that, even a hazy one, you start asking whether a university lab is the best place to walk it.

The second was about what academia can and can't do. A lab is great for ideas, papers, and training students. But embodied intelligence ultimately needs hardware, large-scale data, engineering discipline, and real deployment. Those require resources and an organizational form a lab doesn't really have. I came to feel that if I truly believed in this direction, I had to be willing to take it the whole way, from algorithms to the actual product.

The third was people. I asked myself honestly whether I could bring together a team that covered what I couldn't: hardware, systems engineering, product, and business. The students and collaborators I'd worked with, plus people from industry who were also excited about this moment, made me believe that team was possible.

I'll also admit there was an element of "if not now, then when?" Windows like this don't stay open long. If the field was going to have a breakthrough moment, I wanted to be building in it rather than watching from the sidelines. I knew there would be plenty of risk and plenty I didn't know yet. My judgment was that the direction was right and the timing was close enough, and that the rest we would learn by doing.

r002.rationale: He Wang says he assessed whether he could bring together people to cover his hardware and other capability gaps, and that believing such a team was possible helped him decide to found the company.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a single moment of "I'm ready." It was more like several signals converging, and I had to be honest with myself about each one.

The first signal was technical. By late 2022, I'd been working on 3D vision and robot manipulation at Peking University for years, and we kept hitting the same wall: in the lab, you could demo a grasp or a dexterous hand trick on a few objects, but the moment you changed the scene, everything fell apart. Then two things happened almost at once. Large language models showed that scaling data and compute could produce real generalization, and our own experiments with large-scale synthetic data for grasping were starting to transfer to the real world in a way I hadn't seen before. I remember looking at those results and thinking, the ceiling has moved. The problem isn't whether general manipulation is possible anymore, it's who gets there and how fast.

The second question I asked myself was about data. Everyone says embodied intelligence has no internet to scrape, and that's true. So I had to ask: do I have a concrete thesis for where the data comes from? If my answer had been "we'll collect it with teleoperation and hope," I wouldn't have started. But I did have a thesis, which was simulation first, with a sim-to-real pipeline that we'd already validated in a narrow domain. That gave me a path that didn't depend on raising a billion dollars before producing anything useful.

The third signal was about me personally, and this one was harder. Being a professor and being a founder are very different jobs. In the lab, a result that works eighty percent of the time is a paper. In a company, that's a product nobody buys. So I asked myself whether I could tolerate shifting from "what's interesting" to "what's reliable," and whether I could build a team that complemented me on hardware, on supply chain, on everything academia never taught me. I spent a few months talking to people in industry, to investors, to friends who'd left academia, essentially stress-testing whether I was fooling myself.

And the last factor was timing. In early 2023, capital was starting to pay attention to robotics again, but the field wasn't crowded yet. I felt that if I waited another year or two until the path was obvious, the window for someone with a research background to define the approach would have closed. So in the end, "ready" wasn't a feeling of confidence. It was more that the cost of not trying had become higher than the risk of failing.

astra-6.text:
For me, it wasn’t a question of feeling completely ready. I was asking whether the technology was mature enough to pursue, whether we had a clear starting point, and whether we could build the right team.

In embodied intelligence, a promising research result is only a beginning. You have to get a system to work reliably in the physical world, and then find a use case where that reliability creates value. So I would separate confidence in the long-term direction from confidence in the first product. You need both, but they’re different judgments.

I wouldn’t say I had every uncertainty resolved in early 2023. The threshold was whether there was enough conviction to start, and whether the remaining uncertainties were things we could learn by building.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, being ready didn’t mean that every technical problem had been solved. It meant asking whether I had enough conviction about the direction, whether I could identify a concrete starting point, and whether I could bring together a team capable of making progress.

Embodied intelligence is a very broad ambition. The harder question is: what do you build first, and how do you know it’s working? A research demonstration is one thing; a system that works reliably in the physical world is another. So I would judge readiness by whether we could turn that broad ambition into a cycle of building, testing, and learning.

You can’t remove all the uncertainty before starting. But you do need to distinguish between uncertainty you can work through and assumptions you’re simply hoping will turn out to be true.
